Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the strongest document in the series. It does what the earlier critiques asked for:
- registered hours measures that don't depend on self-report,
- a registered mediation test filed before the outcomes existed,
- a two-year horizon,
- a counter arm that was stopped and reported rather than quietly dropped,
- Halden survivors framed explicitly as an upper bound.

It also corrects both earlier overreaches fairly. Varga–Holm's "entirely an artifact" claim and the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" claim both fail against this evidence.

The arithmetic checks:
- 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8%, and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- For Halden, 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, and 96.8 / 0.866 gives +11.8%.

I'd still want several things fixed. Two of them could change how the decline and the mediation result are read.

## 1. The summary overstates the decline by mixing measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is from timesheets and the 8.5% is from system logs. The body correctly identifies the like-for-like comparison as **12.5% → 9.8%** on timesheets, a fall of about a fifth. Section 5's "about a quarter" sits between the two.

The summary should use the timesheet comparison. It should then report the log-measured 8.5% as a separate refinement.

The decline also isn't tested. The intervals, (6.9 to 18.4) and (4.6 to 15.2), overlap almost entirely. "Consistent with some fading" is fair, but the data are also consistent with no fading. Report a test of the difference.

## 2. The control group changed meeting practice too, which affects the decline

The "unplanned observation" is presented as a side note. It actually bears on the main result. In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut recurring meetings, and their output per hour rose about 4%. That narrows the treated–control gap from month 15 onward.

**Part of the apparent fade from 12.5% to 9.8% may be control offices improving, not treated offices declining.** The report should:
- show treated and control trajectories separately, not only the difference;
- re-estimate with those two offices excluded, or with an indicator for the post-audit period, as a sensitivity check;
- say whether the audit was prompted by contact with treated offices, which would be spillover.

The aggregate control meeting figures also don't obviously reconcile. Control offices averaged 7.2 hours at baseline. Two of them fell from 7.1 to 5.0, yet the control average at month 24 is 7.0. If the offices are equally weighted and these are point-in-time figures, the other five must have *risen* from about 7.2 to about 7.8 hours. That's possible, but it needs stating, or the timing and weighting of the figures needs clarifying.

## 3. What do system logs measure, and do they include meetings?

Logs are described as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases." That definition seems to **exclude meeting time.** The numbers don't fit that reading. On a rough check:
- Treated staff had about 33.4 timesheet hours at month 24, minus 3.9 hours of meetings, giving about 29.5 hours outside meetings.
- Control staff had about 37.9 minus 7.0, giving about 30.9.

That is roughly a 4–5% difference in non-meeting time. If logs captured only casework, log hours should fall by about 4–5%, not 11%. Either logs include time logged in during meetings, or something else differs.

This matters twice:
- **The "stricter measure" claim.** If logs miss meetings, they aren't a stricter version of timesheet hours. They measure something different.
- **The mediation result.** If the denominator includes meeting time, cutting meetings raises output per hour partly by construction. The substantive finding would then be that *meetings could be cut without losing output*, and should be described that way. If the denominator excludes meetings, a meetings pathway must work through something else, such as fewer interruptions, and that needs explaining.

Please define the log measure precisely and reconcile it with the calendar data.

## 4. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result

Registering the mediation analysis before the outcomes existed is good practice. But:

- **Same offices.** The exploratory finding came from these same seven treated offices. A registered test on later data from the same offices guards against analytic flexibility. It isn't an independent replication, and anything particular to these offices carries over.
- **Unit of analysis.** "A larger sample of office-months" suggests office-months may be the unit. With 14 clusters, the 28–66% interval seems narrow. Confirm that inference is clustered by office with small-cluster corrections. I raised the same concern about the nine-month report and it isn't addressed here.
- **Assumptions.** You note the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption. Two further issues:
  - **The mediators aren't independent.** Fewer meetings plausibly reduce fatigue. Say how the shared pathway was allocated, since sequential or joint mediation models give different shares.
  - **Where the baseline meeting data come from.** The nine-month report had calendar data only for month six. Where do the baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2) come from? If they were retrieved from historical calendars, say so and note any coverage gaps.

"Supports" would be accurate. "Confirms" isn't.

## 5. Halden follow-up: nonresponse, and one reversion that wasn't about coverage

- **Nonresponse.** Nine of the 23 contacted organisations didn't provide data. Non-responders after a reversion are likely to be less successful ones, so the true reversion rate among the 23 is probably higher than 3 of 14. The upper-bound framing covers the output figure, but the reversion count should get the same caveat.
- **The marketing agency.** It reverted citing *client deadlines*, not opening hours. Marketing would be coded discretionary in the meta-analysis. Grouping it under "client-facing or coverage obligations" hides an informative case: work that is nominally discretionary but bound to external responsiveness. That supports the meta-analysis's own limitation that a binary work-type coding is too coarse, and it's worth saying so directly.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Sick days are still counted in days.** The −27% has the same possible mechanical component as before. If the 30-hour rotas meant fewer working days, fewer scheduled days produce fewer sick days. Report absence per scheduled hour.
- **Cost.** Output per FTE is −3.4% at unchanged pay, plus overtime, so cost per case has risen by roughly 3.5% or more. The county's question was about cost as much as service, so report it. The counter-arm figure of +9% cost per contact is a county estimate, not a trial result. Label it as such.
- **Appeal overturns.** By 24 months most appeals should have resolved, so 3.2% vs 3.0% is now meaningful. It should still have a confidence interval.
- **Conflicts and tone.** Okafor co-authored the Halden working paper. The Varden authors are evaluating criticism of their own hypothesis. A conflict statement belongs in the paper. "Since dismissed as post hoc" reads as score-settling and could be dropped. The evidence makes the point on its own.
- **Meta-analysis rebuttal.** The claim that all four long studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours is decisive if true. Since it comes from the meta-analysis's supplementary table, cite the table directly so readers can check.

## Overall

Across all six documents, the evidence now points to:

- **Coverage-bound work:** reduced hours lower output and service unless staff are added. The county ended the counter arm at month 12.
- **Discretionary work:** a per-actual-hour gain of roughly **8–10%** that has persisted for two years in a randomised trial. Output per employee is slightly below control, so the hours cut is mostly but not fully offset.
- **Mechanism:** perhaps half the gain is tied to meeting reduction, with a smaller part from fatigue. The definitional issue in point 3 needs resolving first.

The open policy question is the one this trial can't answer. If a meeting audit alone produced a 4% gain in two uncontrolled offices, how much of the 8–10% could employers get **without cutting hours**? Alternatively, is the hours cut what forces reorganisation to happen and stick? The next study should have three arms: reduced hours, reorganisation only (a structured meeting audit), and control. It should measure output per FTE and cost per unit, not only output per hour.

I can draft this as a referee report, or write the cross-study synthesis now that the long-run data are in.
